core_principles.text: Start the lunge in a standing position and then take a step with one foot.
One foot should be in front and one foot should be behind the torso, similar to a split stance.
The feet should be about hip-width apart during the lunge setup.
The distance between the front foot and back foot should be a length that is greater than a walking stride.
The hamstrings and gastrocnemius function as dynamic stabilizers at the knee joint through the lunge movement.
The lunge movement requires the torso to maintain stability in a split stance.
The torso should be straight and the abdominals should be tight.
The scapula should be retracted and depressed with the eyes looking forward.
The toes and knees of both legs should be pointing forward.
The back heel should be off the ground.
Lower the hips until both knees are bent at about a 90-degree angle, if possible.
Make sure the front knee is directly above the ankle and not over the toe.
Push through the front heel to return to the starting position while contracting the glutes, quadriceps, and calves.
The distance between the front foot and back foot should be a length that is greater than a walking stride.
At the lowest point of the downward movement, the hip, knee, and ankle joints should be no less than 90 degrees.
Once in the appropriate starting position, the hips should move down and up in a straight line.
Ensure that the torso maintains an upright, erect posture with the abdominals engaged, chest lifted, and shoulders and back down.

common_mistakes.text: If the feet are too close together, the downward movement results in an increased amount of stress on the knee joint.
Even a slight turn of the lead foot or lead knee inward during a forward lunge can increase the torque stress of the knee joint of the front leg.
Rotating the back knee or foot outward during a forward lunge increases torque stress in the knee joint.
Beginners tend to lean too far forward during the eccentric phase of the exercise.
To compensate for balance and strength challenges, the torso can lean forward during the downward phase, even if the lower body is performing the correct technique.

specific_findings.text: Lower the hips until both knees are bent at about a 90-degree angle, if possible.
At the lowest point of the downward movement, the hip, knee, and ankle joints should be no less than 90 degrees.

consequences.text: If the feet are too close together, the downward movement results in an increased amount of stress on the knee joint, specifically the patellar tendon.

Turning the lead foot or lead knee inward during a forward lunge increases the torque stress of the knee joint of the front leg, which can exacerbate previous knee injuries and lead to increased knee pain.
Rotating the back knee or foot outward during a forward lunge increases torque stress in the knee joint, which can limit performance, exacerbate pre-existing injuries, and potentially cause pain.
Leaning too far forward during the eccentric phase of the exercise can increase the shear force at the knee joint, increasing the risk of injury or pain.

core_principles.text: Performing the lunge with balance support, such as holding on to a stable and non-moving object, reduces the difficulty by increasing the points of contact.
Reducing the range of motion in a lunge can still effectively activate the muscles used, challenge balance, and incorporate functionality.
Performing the lunge from a completely stationary position where the feet do not move until repetitions are completed is an effective modification.
Elevating the front leg a few inches on a box or step decreases stress on the front leg and reduces the difficulty of the lunge.
Using a chair to sit the glute of the front leg down during the lower phase combines support and reduced range of motion.
Alternating lunges that require an opposite step forward for each repetition, or performing walking lunges forward and backward, increases the difficulty.
Side lunges place more mechanical stress on the muscles of the hip joints, specifically the glutes and hamstrings.
Placing a balance disk, wobble board, BOSU ball, or foam pad under the front leg increases instability, forcing stabilizer muscles to activate more and prime movers to work harder.
Adding resistance away from the body, such as holding weight with straight arms overhead, in front, or to the sides, increases the lever length and difficulty.
Performing split squat jumps from a split stance without a forward step increases power.
Learning to lunge correctly can strengthen the lower body musculature, improve core stability and balance, enhance hip flexibility, and increase functionality.
